_comment: Canonical claims: rules this repo must state identically everywhere they are relied on. Each entry pins the EXACT phrasings that count as stating the claim; a carrier contains one or it does not. There is no condition/negation inference — #341 deleted it after 24 review rounds and 100 findings with no downward trend. Read check-claims.js's header before editing: it explains why a phrasing must be long enough that no `mustNotMatch` string contains it, which the guard enforces mechanically at load. Adding a legitimately reworded carrier means adding its wording here — that visible edit IS the design, not a workaround.

claims.why: A clean Codex rerun can arrive as a 👍 reaction or as an INLINE REVIEW-THREAD REPLY, and an inline reply never enters the comment list. A file that says only 'check the comments' sends a session to a gate it cannot clear. Round 35 of #294 found that narrowed form in nine files while the source said both — this claim's best case, and the reason it is pinned. The phrasings carry their connector ('so check …', 'predictable: check …') rather than the bare instruction: with the bare form, inverting automations.md to 'so never check …' PASSED, because a phrasing is a substring of its own negation. Measured on #341, not imagined.

claims.why: Codex-authored and naming the current head proves the run happened, not that it was clean — a review WITH live findings names the head too. Round 36 of #294 fixed the inverted form, which had authorised merging over open findings. The three phrasings are the three carriers' actual wordings; CLAUDE.md states it anaphorically ('a response naming the head is not one'), which is why its wording is listed separately rather than approximated by a shared one.

consumers.why: Found by review, NOT by --derive, and it is the entry's own recorded limit made concrete: this carrier states the claim ANAPHORICALLY — 'a clean current-head Codex verdict — a response naming the head is not one' — where the predicate is the pronoun 'one', pointing back to 'verdict' a clause earlier. Under the old regex this needed a per-consumer override, because no widening reached the pronoun without also matching sentences that are not this claim. Under literal pinning it is simply one more approved phrasing. This is the repo's PRIMARY instruction file and the merge gate it describes is the one that authorises merging over live findings, so it is the last carrier that should have been unlisted.

claims.why: #336 round 5 made every reaction-only round escalate to the owner. Round 6 showed that is wrong for the common case: when a PR's FIRST Codex pass comes back clean as a reaction, codex-monitor never adds `codex-flagged` at all, so the reaction ladder clears the verdict gate, the absent label satisfies the label gate, and the merge proceeds unattended. All five carriers state it in one shared sentence, so one phrasing pins it everywhere.

claims.why: #336 defined the *unreachable-review test* — the one condition under which a session may take `codex-flagged` off by hand — and then spent three consecutive review rounds being shown a consumer that had dropped it. Round 4: the commit that INTRODUCED the name coined two aliases for it in the same breath. A NAME is undone by a suffix rather than by a clause, so each phrasing pins the character that follows it ('test.', 'test admits', 'test, and', 'test:') — that boundary is what keeps 'tests', 'tester', 'testing' and 'test-cases' from counting as the name, and the mustNotMatch entries are exactly those four. ⚠️ Pinning the name cannot see the CONTENT of the rule; `unreachable-review-terminal-states` is the entry that does.

claims.why: ci-notify resolves ONE open PR from a head SHA, else branch plus head-repo owner. The WEAK failure (no unique candidate, so it exits silently) is not the dangerous one and is stated separately in every carrier; the dangerous one is that even a UNIQUE match proves nothing, because a repository_dispatch run carries the DEFAULT-BRANCH SHA and can uniquely match an unrelated promotion PR, which then receives the comment. Every phrasing therefore keeps 'unique' behind its article: 'unique' is a SUBSTRING of 'non-unique', so a carrier regressing to the weak case while wearing the strong case's words would otherwise still count. Both capitalisations are listed because CLAUDE.md opens a sentence with it and the others do not.

claims.why: The counterpart to the wake gap above: when a run could end without waking the session, the check-in is what keeps the PR from being abandoned mid-flight. Rounds 37 and 39 of #294 were both this claim failing to reach a consumer — round 39's was in wait-gate.sh, which states the rule twice and whose DELIVERED message is the copy that matters. Eleven carriers word it eleven ways, which is why there are eleven phrasings and why #341 abandoned trying to infer the shape. Each lowercase one carries its connector: with a bare 'arm the check-in whenever …', inverting CLAUDE.md to 'Never arm the check-in whenever …' PASSED, because ci-notify's lowercase wording matched inside the negation — one carrier's phrasing covering another carrier's inversion.

consumers.why: This file states the rule TWICE — once in its explanatory header comment, once inside the echo the PreToolUse hook actually delivers. The delivered copy carries the most authority: it reaches a session unprompted, at the decision point. Round 39 of #294 was this claim missing here. The header says 'arms a check-in alongside it' and the message says 'ARM A CHECK-IN ALONGSIDE IT', so the phrasing pinned for this claim matches only the delivered form — verified on #341 by deleting the rule from the echo alone, leaving the header intact, and watching the guard go red.
